title: RRSP Basics
summary: CONTRIBUTE → DEDUCT → GROW → PAY TAX LATER
subtitle: An RRSP is a trade. You give up some income now for a tax break today and decades of tax-free growth.

blocks.text: An RRSP is a trade.

You set aside some income now. In exchange, you get a tax break today and years of tax-sheltered growth. The bill comes due later, usually in retirement, when your income and tax rate are often lower.
That’s the whole idea. Everything else in this lesson is detail.
Turn part of today’s tax bill into money that works for your retirement.
blocks.detail: Used in the right years, an RRSP shrinks your tax now and lets your savings grow untaxed for decades.
blocks.extra: Section 05 shows which years make each dollar count most.

sections.title: The mechanics, one step at a time

blocks.text: You contribute, and your taxable income drops. Money you put into an RRSP is deducted from your income. Remember the shelf idea from the Marginal Tax Rates lesson? An RRSP contribution takes income off your top shelf, the one taxed at your highest rate.
It grows, sheltered from tax. Inside the account, your investments grow with no tax on gains, dividends or interest for as long as the money stays in.

You pay tax when you take it out. This is the part people forget. An RRSP is tax-deferred, which means the tax is put off until later. When you withdraw, the money is added to your income and taxed at whatever rate applies then.
The bet built into an RRSP is simple: your tax rate in retirement will likely be lower than in your working years. For most people, that bet pays off.

items.title: “An RRSP is basically the same as a TFSA, just with a different name.”
items.text: They work in opposite directions. An RRSP gives you a deduction now and taxes you later. A TFSA gives you no deduction now but never taxes you again. Mixing them up can lead to a nasty surprise, like thinking an RRSP withdrawal is tax-free.

blocks.text: Taking money out early costs twice. Your bank holds back tax on the spot: 10% on withdrawals up to $5,000, 20% from $5,000 to $15,000, and 30% above that (rates differ in Quebec). The full amount is then added to your income at tax time, so you may owe more. And the room you used is gone for good. Unlike a TFSA, an RRSP doesn’t give withdrawn room back.

sections.title: How much room you actually have

blocks.text: Every year, you build new RRSP room: 18% of what you earned the year before, up to a yearly cap. For 2026, that cap is $33,810.

Most people never get close to the cap. It only matters once your earned income passes about $188,000 the year before. If you belong to a workplace pension, your new room is cut by a pension adjustment.
Room you don’t use doesn’t disappear. It carries forward with no end date, stacking up year after year.
RRSP room in 2026

items.title: New room each year
items.text: 18% — of last year’s earned income, minus any pension adjustment.

items.title: Yearly dollar cap
items.text: $33,810 — the most new room anyone gets for 2026.

items.title: Unused room
items.text: Never expires — it carries forward to future years.

items.title: Over-contribution buffer
items.text: $2,000 — go past your limit by more than this and you pay 1% a month on the excess.

blocks.text: CREDIT PULSE SPOTLIGHT: THE 60-DAY WINDOW EVERYONE HALF-REMEMBERS

Contributions made in the first 60 days of a new year come with a choice. You can claim them on last year’s tax return or a later one, whichever helps more. This matters most if you got a late-year bonus or your income jumped partway through the year. Contribute in January or February, and you can still shrink last year’s taxable income. For the 2025 tax year, the deadline was March 2, 2026. Miss it, and the contribution counts toward this year instead. Not a disaster, just a lost choice.

sections.title: When an RRSP contribution is worth the most

blocks.text: Not every year is equal. Because the deduction is worth more on a higher shelf, an RRSP contribution saves more tax in a high-earning year than a low one.
That’s why timing matters as much as the amount. In an early-career, low-income year, you might get more value from a TFSA, and use your RRSP room later, once your income and shelf have climbed.
There’s no single right answer. It depends on where you sit now and where you expect to sit later.

items.title: “You should always contribute to your RRSP as early as possible in your career.”
items.text: Not always. The deduction is worth more in higher-earning years. Someone on a low shelf early in their career may get more value by saving the room and using it later, once their income and tax rate have grown.

blocks.text: CREDIT PULSE SPOTLIGHT: THE SPOUSAL RRSP NOBODY EXPLAINS

The shelf idea doesn’t stop at one person. If you have a spouse or common-law partner, you can pay into a spousal RRSP: a plan in their name, funded from your own room. You get the deduction. They own the account and pay the tax when the money comes out, years from now. For a couple with a big income gap, this evens out retirement income, so both partners draw at lower rates instead of one person paying a high rate on it all. One catch: if the money comes out within about three calendar years of your last spousal contribution, it is usually taxed in your hands instead. Planned around that timing, it’s one of the most overlooked ways a couple can lower their lifetime tax bill.

Your RRSP has an end date. By December 31 of the year you turn 71, you must turn it into a RRIF or an annuity, or cash it out, which is taxed all at once. The RRIF Basics lesson covers what happens next.

items.title: I know my RRSP deduction limit, checked on my Notice of Assessment, not estimated.
I know roughly which shelf I’m on this year, and whether that makes an RRSP deduction especially valuable right now.
I understand withdrawals are taxed as income later. This is deferred tax, not free money.
If I’m contributing in January or February, I know I can choose which tax year it applies to.
I won’t mix up my RRSP and my TFSA. They work in opposite directions.

blocks.text: Priya’s two decisions
paragraphs: Priya started her first job in Toronto at twenty-two, earning $42,000. Her uncle, who loved giving advice at family dinners, told her to pour everything into her RRSP right away. The earlier, the better, he said.

She put in $3,000 that first year. When she filed her return, the refund was smaller than she had hoped. Her income sat on the bottom shelf, so each dollar she contributed only saved her the lowest rate of tax.

Eight years and two promotions later, Priya was earning $95,000. Her uncle’s advice was still in her head, but she had a different plan for her bonus: a long-promised trip to see her grandmother in Chennai. She almost skipped her RRSP that year. After all, she told herself, she had “done her RRSP” at twenty-two.

Before booking, she sat down with a fee-only planner. He pulled up her shelves. Part of her income now sat on the 20.5% federal shelf, with Ontario’s higher rate stacked on top. Every RRSP dollar she put in this year would save her far more tax than a dollar had at twenty-two.
Priya made her choice. She put $8,000 into her RRSP and used the tax refund to pay for the flight. The rest of her bonus covered the trip itself.

That winter she sat in her grandmother’s kitchen in Chennai, drinking chai. She told her about the uncle, the shelves and the refund that bought her plane ticket. Her grandmother laughed and said the uncle had been right about saving and wrong about the timing.

blocks.text: An RRSP gives you a tax deduction now and taxes you later, ideally at a lower rate in retirement. Room builds every year and never expires. The deduction is worth more in high-earning years, so timing your contributions to your highest shelves often beats contributing early just for the sake of it.
Match your RRSP to your best tax years, and every dollar works harder.
blocks.detail: Contributing when your shelf is high turns the same savings into a bigger refund you can put to work.

blocks.text: Worksheet: your RRSP plan

Answer guidance: if your RRSP limit is a guess, check your Notice of Assessment. It shows the real number. If you’re unsure whether this is a good year to contribute, that’s a fair question for a licensed adviser, since the answer depends on your own income pattern.

items.title: RRSP deduction limit
items.text: The total you can contribute and deduct: this year’s new room plus any unused room carried forward.

items.title: Earned income
items.text: Mainly job and self-employment income, used to work out new RRSP room. Investment income doesn’t count.

items.title: Pension adjustment
items.text: A cut to your RRSP room if you also belong to a workplace pension plan.

items.title: Tax-deferred
items.text: Tax is put off until you withdraw, not removed.

blocks.text: Educational only, not investment advice. Figures are 2026 limits. Confirm current amounts before you contribute.
